whatItDoes.text: Sitting as the Countywide Planning Authority, the board adopted an ordinance changing the countywide land use map for 2.69 acres at 2577 Keystone Road from Residential Rural to Public/Semi-Public. The site already holds a community assembly building, and the change lets the owner replace it with a slightly larger one, with new parking, stormwater work and removal of the current Keystone Road driveway. A companion county zoning overlay limits the site to community assembly with accessory storage; staff listed no fiscal impact.

lg-97655.note: The record lists a state-filed copy of Ordinance 26-26 but no filing date. The companion county map change (FLU-26-01) was approved June 16, 2026, before this vote.

whatItDoes.text: Approved an agreement of up to $25 million with Operation PAR, Inc. to build and run a walk-in behavioral health urgent care center offering same-day mental health and addiction care, through September 30, 2030. The money comes entirely from regional opioid lawsuit settlement funds held in a separate fund, not the General Fund; staff estimated about $3.4 million for building costs, $2.7 million for start-up and $6.2 million a year for three years of services. A land use restriction requires the property to be used for substance use prevention, treatment or related services through October 1, 2046.

behavioral-urgent-care.note: The staff summary does not give the center's address or opening date.

whatItDoes.text: Hired American Infrastructure Development, Inc. as the county's owner's representative on the passenger terminal improvements at St. Pete-Clearwater International Airport, for up to $1,742,865.82 over 2,320 days after a notice to proceed. The firm oversees design review, bidding, coordination with the FAA, TSA and the construction manager, full-time inspection, and pay requests and change orders. The cost is paid from the airport's revenue and operating fund, and about 17% goes to two certified small business subcontractors.

Gave final approval to the property tax rates and budgets for the year that began October 1, 2026, including a General Fund budget of $1.121 billion. The countywide General Fund rate is 4.4989 mills ($4.4989 per $1,000 of taxable value), down from 4.5423 mills the year before, and the Health Department rate stays at 0.0713 mills. Because both are slightly above the rolled-back rate (the rate that would raise the same tax money as last year), state law lists the combined 4.5702 mills as a 0.73% property tax increase.

At the first of two budget hearings, the board set tentative tax rates and budgets for the year starting October 1, 2026, and cut the proposed countywide General Fund rate from 4.5423 mills to 4.4989 mills. It also approved budget changes that included $667,000 in one-time reserve money for social action funding. Tentative rates are the ceiling for the final vote two weeks later.

afterward.text: At the final budget hearing the board adopted the General Fund rate of 4.4989 mills.

fy27-tentative.note: The county's 'fifth cut in six years' description was not found in the records opened.

whatItDoes.text: Awarded three five-year contracts, starting October 1, 2026, to run rental car counters for five brands at St. Pete-Clearwater International Airport: Alamo; Enterprise and National; and Avis and Budget. These contracts bring money in rather than spend it; staff estimated $28,210,137.70 in revenue to the airport fund over 60 months. They replace contracts the board approved in March 2022.

airport-rental-cars.note: The input's $8.5 million to $10.4 million range was not found; the staff report gives a single 60-month revenue estimate of $28.2 million.

whatItDoes.text: Approved two property owners' petition to vacate an unbuilt 33-foot strip of Portsmouth Road right-of-way behind their home at 1725 Doncaster Road, next to Gulf Breeze Estates. The county gives up its public road claim to the strip, which was never built and has no public access; staff said there is no future need and the utilities raised no objection. Staff listed no fiscal impact.

lg-97157.note: The record lists recorded and re-recorded copies of Resolution 26-65 without dates.

whatItDoes.text: Set the highest property tax rates the county could adopt for the year starting October 1, 2026; these went on the TRIM notices mailed to owners on August 17. The countywide General Fund rate (4.5423 mills) and 20 other rates stayed at current levels, the Seminole Fire Rescue District ceiling rose from 1.8000 to 1.9581 mills, and the Pinellas Planning Council rate fell from 0.0175 to 0.0171 mills. The board could lower these rates later but not practically raise them.

afterward.text: At the first budget hearing the board lowered the proposed General Fund rate from 4.5423 to 4.4989 mills.
Final rates were adopted with the General Fund at 4.4989 mills; the county's hearing schedule listed the Seminole Fire District at 1.9499 mills, below the 1.9581 ceiling.

trim-max.note: No Legistar vote record; the consensus is documented by the County Administrator report and presentation.

whatItDoes.text: Raised the yearly trash collection charge on Lealman residential tax bills from $240 to $288 per home, a $48 increase, and certified the roll so the Tax Collector can bill it. Staff said the charge pays only for Lealman collection, disposal and district costs (not the General Fund) and builds reserves before the current collection contract ends December 31, 2026; it estimated $2,136,880 in revenue for 2027. The staff report said the new collection contract will cost $264 per home per year.

afterward.text: The board added $670,000 to the current Coastal Waste and Recycling contract through December 31, 2026, mainly to cover 415 more customers added since 2021 and to reconcile the first three months of the 2016 contract; the record says the new Waste Management contract begins January 1, 2027.

whatItDoes.text: Set the fee for dumping trash at the county's solid waste facility at $63.57 per ton from October 1, 2026, and $68.65 per ton from October 1, 2027, 8% increases each year from $58.86. Staff said the increases follow a rate study and partly replace revenue lost when the county's power sale agreement with Duke Energy ended in December 2024, which had paid $77,361,750 in FY24. Tipping fees are budgeted to bring in $64,175,640 in FY27, $4,753,760 more than FY26.

Amended the county towing ordinance, which caps what tow companies may charge. As proposed by staff it adds a yearly inflation adjustment to base tow rates capped at 3% for five years, a $1 per mile emergency fuel surcharge when diesel tops $5.50 a gallon, an electric vehicle fee of $35 per 15 minutes on scene (up to $70), a $70 after-hours gate fee, higher rates for larger vehicles, photo or video before a tow, new signs at private tow sites, and limits on when lien fees can start. The board approved it as amended, so the final text may differ from the staff proposal; staff said it brings no revenue to the county.

lg-96842.note: The specific amendments made at the meeting were not in the records opened; the state-filed Ordinance 26-21 was not read.

whatItDoes.text: Raised the county's maximum towing rates for cars and light trucks (Class A) through Resolution 26-46: a private property trespass tow goes to $175 flat (from $147), plus up to $6 a mile for up to 10 miles, and daily storage goes to $35 (from $30). Police-directed tows are capped at $153 plus $5 a mile. These caps do not cover the separate lien release fee of up to $250 that state law allows tow companies to charge.

afterward.text: The board amended the towing ordinance itself, adding an inflation adjustment, fuel surcharge, electric vehicle fee and other changes.

lg-96804.note: The input's '$60 mileage rate' matches the resolution's $6 per mile for up to 10 miles.

whatItDoes.text: Approved a term sheet, an outline of deal terms, for redeveloping Clearwater's BayCare Ballpark, Phillies Complex and Carpenter Complex so the Phillies and Clearwater Threshers keep using them through 2047. The county would contribute $85 million, expected to come from the Tourist Development Tax Fund rather than property taxes, and the Phillies would pay the county tourism agency $850,000 a year for marketing starting in 2026, rising 3% a year from 2032. The term sheet spends no money by itself; the final agreements must come back to the board.

lg-96263.note: No final Phillies agreements were found in Legistar as of October 27, 2026.

whatItDoes.text: Rewrote the rules for the program that gives tourist development tax money to local building projects that draw visitors. The board now sets the total pot each round; beach park facilities became eligible; projects need matching money in hand and at least 25,000 visitors and 10,000 hotel room nights a year (beach parks exempt); projects that miss the rules or ask more than $10 million can no longer request a board exception; and the point system was dropped while keeping the same evaluation criteria. The change spends no money by itself.

afterward.text: Under the new rules the board set a $30.6 million maximum for the FY26 funding round: $15.3 million for regular capital projects and $15.3 million for beach park facilities.

lg-95280.note: The input's description of a removed geographic-spread point category was not found; staff said the defined point system was eliminated but the evaluation criteria were kept.

whatItDoes.text: Formally adopted by resolution a solid waste tipping fee of $58.86 per ton, effective October 1, 2025, an 8% increase from $54.50 that was already part of the FY26 budget approved in September 2025. Staff said it is the first of three planned 8% yearly increases to partly replace lost Duke Energy capacity payments, and budgeted $59,421,880 in FY26 tipping fee revenue.

afterward.text: The board adopted the next two increases: $63.57 per ton for FY27 and $68.65 per ton for FY28.

whatItDoes.text: Denied, without prejudice, Green Energy for North America, LLC's request to change 18.43 acres at 13400 Pine Street in unincorporated Largo, a former construction debris landfill, from Residential Urban (up to 7.5 homes per acre, about 138 units) to Residential Medium (up to 15 per acre, about 276 units). The land keeps its current designation, and without prejudice means the owner may apply again. County staff recommended denial, citing fit with nearby single-family neighborhoods and no binding site plan or affordability terms; the Local Planning Agency also recommended denial, 4 to 2.

Amended the 2026 list of events paid for with tourist development tax money so the $65,000 already set for the MLK Dream Parade, now under a new event owner, also covers the Tampa Bay Collard Green Festival. The program total stays at $2,755,000, which reflects $85,000 in staff-level awards made after the board approved the original 49 events; this vote added no new money.

afterward.text: Under authority delegated by the board, the County Administrator approved a $65,000 tourism promotion agreement with The Tampa Bay Collard Green Festival, Inc. for the St. Petersburg MLK Parade / 45 Days of Excellence (January 19 to February 14, 2026).

lg-95249.note: The headline's 'raised funding to $2.76 million' reflects earlier staff actions; this vote itself did not change the total.

whatItDoes.text: Renewed the five-year agreement under which the county pays part of the salaries and benefits of UF/IFAS Extension staff in Pinellas, who run agriculture, 4-H and youth, natural resource and marine programs. The county pays 40% for the director and four agents, 47% for a resources management agent and 5% of one support position, an estimated $297,986.45 a year from the General Fund, billed quarterly. The agreement can end if the county does not budget the money.

Hired Horne LLP to manage and carry out the county's federal disaster recovery grant program (CDBG-DR), funded by $813 million awarded through HUD, under a 36-month contract of up to $565,656,023.17. That total includes up to $25.6 million for program implementation, up to $61.2 million for managing the housing program, and up to $478.9 million in grant money passed through to pay contractors for home repairs and rebuilding, which the firm may not mark up.

afterward.text: A first amendment recorded that the firm was acquired and renamed BDO Government Services LLC, with no change in cost.

The board approved staff's CDBG-DR policy recommendations except three: expanding reimbursement eligibility to multifamily structure types, raising the maximum reimbursement award for mobile home units, and creating a relocation pathway for certain mobile home owners in the Homeowner Rehabilitation Program.

whatItDoes.text: Gave final approval to the property tax rates and budgets for the year that began October 1, 2025. The countywide General Fund rate was set at 4.5423 mills and the General Fund budget at $1,111,851,980. The rate is above the rolled-back rate of 4.4151 mills, which state law counts as a 2.88% property tax increase.

afterward.text: The 4.5423 mill rate was kept as the ceiling for the next year's budget.
For FY27 the board lowered the General Fund rate to 4.4989 mills.

whatItDoes.text: Adopted tentative tax rates and budgets for the year starting October 1, 2025, for the General Fund, Health Department, EMS, the Planning Council, local taxing units and 12 fire districts, after first amending the budget as the County Administrator recommended. The county's hearing presentation shows the General Fund rate moving from 4.5947 mills proposed to 4.5580 mills going into this hearing, through cuts such as smaller risk and fleet reserves. Tentative rates set the ceiling for the final vote on September 18.

afterward.text: The board adopted a final General Fund rate of 4.5423 mills.

whatItDoes.text: Commissioner Scherer, seconded by Commissioner Nowicki, moved a General Fund rate of 4.5049 mills, described as a 50% rollback; that is halfway between the proposed 4.5947 mills and the rolled-back rate of 4.4151 mills. Because the motion failed, that lower rate was not adopted and the board went on to approve the higher tentative rate.

afterward.text: The final General Fund rate adopted was 4.5423 mills.

lg-94414.note: The rolled-back rate cited is from the September 18 final schedule. The input's '$5 million away' remark was not found in the records opened.

whatItDoes.text: Certified the 2025 Lealman trash collection charge at $288 per home, up $48 (20%) from $240, so the Tax Collector could bill Lealman residential owners on their tax bills. Staff said the increase would cover contract costs and build reserves before the collection contract expires; the charge pays only for Lealman trash service and does not come from the General Fund.

afterward.text: The board re-certified the 2025 Lealman roll without the rate increase originally proposed.
The board adopted a resolution raising the charge to $288 per home for 2026.

lg-93830.note: Per the September 11, 2025 record, the $288 charge approved in this vote does not appear to have been billed for 2025.

whatItDoes.text: Approved a five-year contract of up to $1,936,600 (about $387,320 a year) with Keep Pinellas Beautiful, Inc. to run the county's volunteer cleanup programs: Adopt-A-Trail, Adopt-A-Mile, Adopt-A-Pond, litter control and education, and SeeClickFix litter reports. Over the term Solid Waste pays $1,500,110, Public Works $318,985 and Parks $117,505; it replaced a contract expiring August 10, 2025.

Approved up to $2,685,000 in tourist development tax money for 49 events in the 2026 budget year, including $250,000 each for the Firestone Grand Prix of St. Petersburg and the Valspar Championship, $150,000 for St. Pete Pride and $75,000 for the Clearwater Jazz Festival. Another $315,000 of the $3 million program could go to later events or marketing, and county staff sign the individual event agreements.

afterward.text: The board revised the FY26 list; the program total stood at $2,755,000 after staff-level awards.

whatItDoes.text: Found that blight conditions exist in about 767 acres of central Tarpon Springs, from the existing downtown redevelopment area east to US 19, set that area as the Central Tarpon Springs Community Redevelopment Area, and gave the city authority to write a redevelopment plan. The vote committed no county money; if the board later approves a plan and trust fund, part of the future growth in county property taxes from the area (at least 50% of it, under the 2021 county policy) would go to projects there.

lg-93179.note: No Central Tarpon Springs redevelopment plan or trust fund approval was found in Legistar through October 2026.

whatItDoes.text: Adopted Resolution 25-34, which directed the County Administrator to start withdrawing the county from Duke Energy's Clean Energy Connection solar program, barred buying electric vehicles (other than utility carts) without a financial analysis reviewed by the board, and dropped the county targets of 50% renewable energy by 2030, 100% for county operations by 2040 and 100% countywide by 2050. It repealed Resolutions 20-146 and 21-127 and took effect October 1, 2025. The resolution states that the program's estimated $15.18 million in savings over 33 years was backloaded and overstated its value.

lg-93001.note: No later record of the withdrawal being completed was found.

whatItDoes.text: Rezoned about 3.2 acres at 2281 Kersey Road and 1736 Winchester Road in unincorporated Largo to R-3-CO single-family residential, allowing up to 11 home lots instead of the 7 allowed under 2021 conditions on the southern parcel. The adopted conditions cut the minimum lot width from 80 to 70 feet, drop the 9,500 square foot minimum lot size, keep larger setbacks on the east and south sides, and add a 10-foot landscape buffer along the east line. It took effect along with a companion land use map change approved the same day.

Approved, as amended, tourist development tax funding of up to $26.4 million for five building projects: the Eddie C. Moore Complex, Clearwater Beach Municipal Marina, Clearwater Marine Aquarium, Palladium Theater and the Arts Center and Chihuly Collection. Staff had recommended $24,785,000; later county records show the marina amount was raised from $7.35 million to $7.85 million. No money is committed until separate agreements are approved, and payment is normally a reimbursement when each project is finished.

afterward.text: The board made the legal finding that the marina is needed to increase tourist business, required before tourist tax money can fund it.
The board approved a $2.5 million funding agreement with St. Petersburg College for the Palladium Theater.
The board approved agreements with Clearwater for $7.85 million for the marina and $7.75 million for the Eddie C. Moore Complex.
The board approved a $6.05 million agreement with the Clearwater Marine Aquarium, waiving the rule to allow milestone payments.

lg-92807.note: The individual amendments other than the marina increase were not found; listed per-project amounts sum to less than $26.4 million.

whatItDoes.text: Adopted a bond resolution and approved the financing documents for the county's share of a new Tampa Bay Rays stadium in St. Petersburg's Historic Gas Plant District, committing the county to yearly debt payments on up to $335 million in bonds for up to 31 years. Repayment comes from the tourist development tax on hotel and other short-term stays, not property taxes. A companion budget change recognized the bond money and moved $39.7 million from tourist tax reserves for issuance costs, reserves and the first year of payments.

afterward.text: The Rays said they could not move forward with the new ballpark. Construction Dive reported that owner Stuart Sternberg cited a series of events beginning in October 2024, and that team leaders had written that the county's earlier bond delay put construction at risk.

rays-bonds.note: Staff records give an upper limit of $335 million, not the $312.5 million in the input headline. No record of bonds being issued was found.

whatItDoes.text: Chose, for 2025, not to give the optional Live Local Act property tax break on county taxes: a 75% exemption for rental units in complexes of 71 or more units rented to households earning 80% to 120% of area median income. The county could opt out because a Shimberg Center report found a surplus of affordable units for that income range in the Tampa Bay metro area. The required 100% exemption for units serving households at or below 80% of median income was not affected.

afterward.text: The board renewed the opt-out for 2026 (Resolution 25-138).

whatItDoes.text: Turned down the neighboring owners' (the Myrbacks') request for a public hearing to appeal a county dredge and fill permit issued July 19, 2024, for 106 Harbor Drive in Palm Harbor, which allows dredging of state-owned submerged land around a private dock and boat lift. With no hearing, the permit stands as issued; staff said it was properly issued after the dredge area was reduced to avoid seagrass.
Chose the board's leaders for 2025: Vice-Chair Scott as chair and Commissioner Eggers as vice chair.

afterward.text: The board chose Vice-Chair Eggers as chair and Commissioner Latvala as vice chair for 2026.
